assumptions: The family company may approve a fully arm's-length pilot without supplying unconsented customer data or free operational resources.
A material portion of callback costs is caused by detectable commissioning settings rather than equipment defects or installation work outside the product's scope.
The initial checklist and uploaded-log service can operate without regulated professional activity by the founder.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A consented prospective pilot across at least 20 installations measuring baseline and post-intervention callback rates, technician time, travel cost, documentation time, false alerts, and installer willingness to pay, followed by repeat paid use outside the family company.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Cross-brand commissioning evidence linked to subsequent callbacks could expose correctable installation patterns that OEM tools miss, but the cited product-registration change does not itself establish a commissioning-quality gap.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Callbacks consume installer labor and travel and therefore offer a clear measurable loss, but incidence, preventability, current documentation burden, and willingness to pay 150-400 PLN per job are all unknown.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Per-installation revenue plus monitoring can repeat and onboarding can be prepaid, but sensors, specialist review, fragmented integrations, support, and liability may undermine the assumed 55-75% contribution margin and high-volume wealth path.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Regional multi-brand Polish installers are a defined and accessible beachhead, including a possible arm's-length pilot, though the subset with enough preventable callbacks is not quantified.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: OEMs already provide commissioning and diagnostics and control device APIs. An independent cross-brand dataset is differentiated but would require broad installer adoption before becoming a strong position.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: Validated commissioning data could support fleet monitoring, predictive maintenance, warranty evidence, installer benchmarking, training, and other HVAC or renewable equipment.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Commissioning-to-callback outcome data could compound into useful benchmarks, but access is consent-dependent, nonexclusive, and vulnerable to OEM integration restrictions or copying.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Cross-brand proof packs and remote review could save visits and standardize quality, but no controlled pilot demonstrates callback reduction, time savings, or superior diagnostic accuracy.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Tighter eligible-device registration supports general quality awareness, but it concerns product eligibility rather than commissioning and therefore supplies only indirect momentum.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The family renewable business may enable a lawful first pilot and wholesalers could aggregate installers, but no rights or commitments exist and wider installer sales remain relationship-driven.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: Checklist-only pilots fit the founder's skills, capital, and part-time schedule, but production requires HVAC expertise, installer behavior change, telemetry access, consent, warranty boundaries, and safe recommendations.

highest_value_structural_change: Make verified callback reduction the product and contract with a wholesaler or multi-brand installer network for outcome data and distribution, rather than anchoring demand on subsidy documentation.
main_structural_strength: A potential first pilot is unusually accessible and could create a cross-brand commissioning-to-outcome dataset with recurring per-installation use.
primary_score_limiter: The evidence does not show that preventable commissioning defects are common or that installers will pay enough for an independent layer over OEM tools.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: The ZUM/EPREL change addresses product eligibility, not commissioning defects, and single-brand installers may already be adequately served by OEM commissioning applications.
